common_errors.cause: Student forgets weight, tension, or a reaction force.
common_errors.correction: List every external force acting on the isolated particle before writing equations.
common_errors.description: Student omits one or more forces from the free-body diagram.

common_errors.cause: Student treats a 2D problem as if one direction were unconstrained.
common_errors.correction: Write and solve both ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
common_errors.description: Student satisfies only one equilibrium equation and ignores the other.

common_errors.cause: Student does not track whether a force acts in the + or - coordinate direction.
common_errors.correction: Return to the FBD and assign signs before writing equilibrium equations.
common_errors.description: Student uses correct magnitudes but wrong signs on one or more components.

common_errors.cause: Student fails to resolve the unknown into x and y parts.
common_errors.correction: Represent angled unknown forces with two component unknowns or magnitude-direction form.
common_errors.description: Student treats an angled unknown force as if it had only one component.

concept.core_idea: Draw the FBD, resolve forces into components, then enforce ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
concept.physical_interpretation: Equilibrium means every push or pull is exactly balanced by other forces in both horizontal and vertical directions.
plain_language: A particle in equilibrium does not accelerate, so the net force on it is zero.
In two dimensions, that means the sum of force components in x and in y must each equal zero.
A free-body diagram isolates the particle and shows every force acting on it.
Unknown forces or angles are found by solving the two equilibrium equations simultaneously.
concept.title: Two-Dimensional Particle Equilibrium

problem.description: A particle is acted on by a 100 N force to the right and a 75 N force upward. A third force F3 keeps the particle in equilibrium. Determine the magnitude of F3.

solution_steps.work: Draw the particle with F1 to the right, F2 upward, and F3 as the unknown balancing force.
Use +x to the right and +y upward.
Components: F1x = 100 N, F1y = 0; F2x = 0, F2y = 75 N; F3x and F3y unknown.
Equilibrium: ΣFx = 100 + F3x = 0 so F3x = -100 N; ΣFy = 75 + F3y = 0 so F3y = -75 N.
Check: 100 - 100 = 0 and 75 - 75 = 0; F3 points down and to the left, which balances the given forces.

worked_example.title: Balancing force for a particle in 2D equilibrium
